sources.title: AI That Works #68 SlopCodeBench
sources.note: Full transcript, README, meta read. Dex presents SlopCodeBench results; Vaibhav asks questions.

sources.title: AI That Works #69 Unconference RECAP
sources.note: Full transcript, README, meta read. Mix of Dex and Vaibhav; many ideas are other attendees' and relayed.

sources.title: AI That Works #70 syncs and A/B testing 200 agents
sources.note: Full transcript, README, meta read. Avery (Boundary) and Kyle Mistele (HumanLayer) present; Dex mostly interjects. Sync-engine half is off-topic for the harness.

cards.author: Dex
cards.quote: you solve all the new challenges, but you break something from number three, then you fail the strict pass
cards.claim: Grade on strict pass (current checkpoint passes and every earlier one still passes), not isolated pass, because regressions are the real failure.
cards.evidence_detail: Benchmark design; GPT-5.4 Codex won isolated pass while Opus 4.6 won strict pass in the March run.
cards.landing: Reviewer per-PR check: earlier phases' register ids still pass at the head SHA, not only the new one
cards.inventory_ref: (B) August 2026 - AI That Works #68 SlopCodeBench

cards.author: Dex
cards.quote: software is really discovering problems as you go. but most benchmarks just give you the whole problem up front
cards.claim: Evaluate agents on increasing requirements over a code base they inherit, measuring both whether it works today and whether it stays easy to extend.
cards.evidence_detail: Motivation for SlopCodeBench; 'position and velocity' framing; checkpoints up to 8 deep.
cards.landing: Phase-sequence trials where each phase inherits the previous phase's repo state
cards.inventory_ref: (B) August 2026 - AI That Works #68 SlopCodeBench

cards.author: Dex
cards.quote: the best models at our time are only getting 33%
cards.claim: Best current models reach only about 33% strict pass (Sol and Fable tied; GPT-5.5 14.8%), so multi-checkpoint work is far from solved.
cards.evidence_detail: Six challenges, one run each, stated not statistically significant; Opus 5 23-25% in the earlier run, Sonnet 5 and Opus 4.8 about 6%.
cards.landing: Calibration for how much unattended multi-phase work to trust
cards.inventory_ref: (B) August 2026 - AI That Works #68 SlopCodeBench

cards.author: Dex
cards.quote: Fable did a little bit better, two percent better, but it cost five times as much.
cards.claim: Spending roughly 5x more bought about 2 points less defect rate; the cost-vs-defect curve flattens toward an asymptote.
cards.evidence_detail: Aggregate cost vs defect-rate chart across six challenges; some models are not directly comparable (different challenge sets).
cards.landing: Model/effort routing for verifiers and implementers
cards.inventory_ref: (B) August 2026 - AI That Works #68 SlopCodeBench

cards.author: Dex
cards.quote: those perform pretty much exactly the same.
cards.claim: The benchmark's 'just solve' prompt and 'plan then implement' prompt scored about the same, so a plan step did not show a measurable gain.
cards.evidence_detail: Dex says he only skimmed the results and puts 'a big asterisk' on it; relays the paper's finding.
cards.landing: Phase routine: whether a mandatory plan step earns its cost
cards.inventory_ref: (B) August 2026 - AI That Works #68 SlopCodeBench

cards.author: Dex
cards.quote: planning was a way to get the model to work for longer.
cards.claim: Plans used to work mainly by keeping the model working unattended; models are now RL'd to keep going, so that benefit of planning is gone.
cards.evidence_detail: Dex's account of the 15-to-10-months-ago planning wave; no data.
cards.landing: Rationale for what the ship-plan phase routine is actually buying (scope control vs endurance)
cards.inventory_ref: (B) August 2026 - AI That Works #68 SlopCodeBench

cards.author: Dex
cards.quote: launch a sub agent to do part one, then I'm gonna check it, then launch another sub agent
cards.claim: What worked better than one long run was doing one plan part at a time, each in its own context, checking between parts.
cards.evidence_detail: Stated as how practice evolved; Ralph-style per-phase fresh context.
cards.landing: One phase per new session in the routine; per-phase sub-agent with checks between
cards.inventory_ref: (B) August 2026 - AI That Works #68 SlopCodeBench

cards.author: Dex
cards.quote: they have to make it as generic as possible, versus you being able to just tell it
cards.claim: Harness-provided plan mode prompts are generic; telling the model exactly which file with which sections to write ('ask me questions until we're aligned, then write a doc like this') beats them, and the design concept in the head should be written down.
cards.evidence_detail: Discussion of Brooks 'design concept' locked in the context window and never written to a file.
cards.landing: Custom plan template in the phase routine rather than built-in plan mode
cards.inventory_ref: (B) August 2026 - AI That Works #68 SlopCodeBench

cards.author: Dex
cards.quote: the next challenge in the new context window will see the scripts and be like, we test this with scripts.
cards.claim: Whatever pattern the first checkpoint sets (e.g. ad hoc scripts instead of unit tests) is copied by every later fresh-context checkpoint.
cards.evidence_detail: Explains why only Sol wrote Python unit tests while the other models used scripts; offered as a theory, mechanism not verified.
cards.landing: Early-phase exemplars and conventions (what the first phases leave in the repo steer later phases)
cards.inventory_ref: (B) August 2026 - AI That Works #68 SlopCodeBench

cards.author: Dex
cards.quote: ninety-five percent of the code written by Saul triggered at least one slop.
cards.claim: Slop detectors (200+ Python AST rules) are aggressive and best used to compare models, not as an absolute bad-code verdict; cyclomatic complexity and cloned-line percentage were the most informative.
cards.evidence_detail: 95% of Sol's lines hit at least one rule; Kimi K3 had >5x cyclomatic complexity growth checkpoint 3 to 8; models otherwise clustered closely.
cards.landing: Deterministic complexity/duplication metrics as backpressure signals in CI
cards.inventory_ref: (B) August 2026 - AI That Works #68 SlopCodeBench

cards.author: Dex
cards.quote: Opus Vrote thirty thousand lines of code for half as many challenges and fifteen thousand lines of tests.
cards.claim: Models write very large volumes of code; a six-challenge run costs about $200 at API prices, and one run is not enough, a proper run would repeat five times and average.
cards.evidence_detail: Opus 5 wrote ~30k lines plus ~15k lines of tests for half the challenges; Dex used subscriptions so cost figures are approximate; single run per model.
cards.landing: Budgeting verifier/refuter runs; repeat-and-average before trusting a comparison
cards.inventory_ref: (B) August 2026 - AI That Works #68 SlopCodeBench

cards.author: Dex
cards.quote: the frontier model has to set up the code base in a way that a small model can solve the next problem.
cards.claim: A 'super strict pass': after a frontier model finishes a checkpoint, a smaller model must ace the next checkpoint on that code base; success is evidence the code base is maintainable enough to go lights-off.
cards.evidence_detail: Dex's proposed next benchmark variant (e.g. a small open model solving checkpoint N+1); not yet run.
cards.landing: Cold-resume style trial: a cheaper/fresh agent must continue from repository state alone
cards.inventory_ref: (B) August 2026 - AI That Works #68 SlopCodeBench

cards.author: Dex
cards.quote: they apply deterministic litters as a feedback loop during the challenge.
cards.claim: Real lights-off factories gate the model with deterministic linters (e.g. a cyclomatic-complexity cap) plus a second model's review, so a fair benchmark should include those loops.
cards.evidence_detail: Third proposed benchmark addition; Dex is unsure whether it helps or hurts.
cards.landing: CI gates such as complexity caps and import-boundary contracts
cards.inventory_ref: (B) August 2026 - AI That Works #68 SlopCodeBench

cards.author: Dex
cards.quote: It might make them worse if you say, Hey, every time Fable writes a thing we have Soul review it
cards.claim: Cross-model review as a standing gate is unproven and could make results worse rather than better.
cards.evidence_detail: Stated as an open question ('very curious to see'); no data.
cards.landing: Opus reviewer per PR; refuter design
cards.inventory_ref: (B) August 2026 - AI That Works #68 SlopCodeBench

cards.author: Dex
cards.quote: the skills exist to give the model things that are not in the weights.
cards.claim: Keep skills only for knowledge the model cannot have (your type system, repo layout, branch named canary); instructions the model already follows, like 'run tests after every change', should go.
cards.evidence_detail: His team threw out an agent-browser skill and would never add a GitHub CLI skill because the model already gets them right.
cards.landing: CLAUDE.md trim criterion and skill admission test (information, not instruction)
cards.inventory_ref: (B) August 2026 - AI That Works #68 SlopCodeBench

cards.author: Dex
cards.quote: You don't need that anymore because the models just do it.
cards.claim: Lines like 'always run the tests after every change' that people put in CLAUDE.md no longer pay for themselves in current models.
cards.evidence_detail: Illustrative example given while explaining which skills and rules to retire.
cards.landing: CLAUDE.md trim: audit for rules current models already follow
cards.inventory_ref: (B) August 2026 - AI That Works #68 SlopCodeBench

cards.author: Dex
cards.quote: you're actually detuning the model and like lowering your performance by having extra instructions in there.
cards.claim: Informational context (facts the model cannot know) carries across model generations; procedural instructions the model can work out itself can detune it, so re-review both at every model release.
cards.evidence_detail: Information-versus-instruction distinction from a mock-up; Dex does not go as far as 'throw everything out' (the advice he attributes to Boris Cherny).
cards.landing: Sort each CLAUDE.md line as information vs instruction; re-audit on model change
cards.inventory_ref: (B) August 2026 - AI That Works #68 SlopCodeBench

cards.author: Dex
cards.quote: do not invoke this skill unless the user requests it by name.
cards.claim: New models over-invoke skills, so about 80% of his team's skill descriptions were rewritten from 'you must use this skill if X' to 'do not invoke unless asked by name'.
cards.evidence_detail: Stated as 80% of skills changed after Sol and Fable; no measurement.
cards.landing: Skill description wording for the skills being added now
cards.inventory_ref: (B) August 2026 - AI That Works #68 SlopCodeBench

cards.author: Dex
cards.quote: don't just cargo cult all your skills from model to model
cards.claim: Re-validate skills, CLAUDE.md and prompts when a new model ships rather than carrying them over, and shared skills need evals.
cards.evidence_detail: Responds to Boris Cherny's throw-it-all-out advice; Dex agrees with 'You need evals on that' for team-wide skills.
cards.landing: Model-change checklist; evals for any shared skill
cards.inventory_ref: (B) August 2026 - AI That Works #68 SlopCodeBench

cards.author: Dex
cards.quote: You can tell your codex model to use the claude CLI.
cards.claim: Automatic cross-model review can be orchestrated with a bash script, a Ralph loop, or simply telling one agent CLI to call the other.
cards.evidence_detail: Answer to a chat question; also mentions Greptile reviewing with the other vendor's model.
cards.landing: Reviewer or refuter step that shells out to a second model
cards.inventory_ref: (B) August 2026 - AI That Works #68 SlopCodeBench

cards.author: Dex
cards.quote: every single thing in the harness can inf influence this outcome.
cards.claim: Harness choices (code-search MCP, extra skills, grep vs indexed search) all shift results and are cheap to test by customising the open harness used by the benchmark.
cards.evidence_detail: Answer to a question on MCP/skills; notes SlopCodeBench runs Sol in Codex CLI, Fable in Claude Code, Kimi in OpenCode, so harness is confounded with model.
cards.landing: Measure harness changes on a fixed task set before adopting them
cards.inventory_ref: (B) August 2026 - AI That Works #68 SlopCodeBench

cards.author: other
cards.quote: give the whole spec up front of every single problem and then I try and solve it.
cards.claim: Compare incremental checkpoints against the full spec given at once; if the latter is much better, the edge is in predicting requirements. Dex says he will add it to the benchmark but argues best product engineers ship small and iterate.
cards.evidence_detail: Vaibhav's hypothesis; Dex: 'I think I'm gonna incorporate that' while disagreeing on the underlying belief.
cards.landing: nowhere obvious
cards.inventory_ref: (B) August 2026 - AI That Works #68 SlopCodeBench

cards.author: Dex
cards.quote: what code do you still have to read, what code can you not read
cards.claim: The frontier question for software factories in 2026 is which code must still be read and how to maximise confidence while avoiding an unrecoverable outage.
cards.evidence_detail: Framing statement in the closing discussion.
cards.landing: Owner review policy and what the one-page owner view surfaces
cards.inventory_ref: (B) August 2026 - AI That Works #68 SlopCodeBench

cards.author: Dex
cards.quote: everyone accepts that if you let models like like run unattended, they will write slop code
cards.claim: Unattended models always write slop, so a team must either accept it or build something against it.
cards.evidence_detail: Dex's summary of the whole unconference; Vaibhav agrees nobody disagreed.
cards.landing: Rationale for backpressure and per-PR review
cards.inventory_ref: (B) August 2026 - AI That Works #69 Unconference Recap

cards.author: other
cards.quote: they don't update their agent's memory, they don't update their prompts or their skills, they actually just go build another linter
cards.claim: One attendee vibe-coded about 70 deterministic Rust linters and, for each recurring anti-pattern, adds a linter that feeds the error back to the agent instead of editing prompts or memory.
cards.evidence_detail: Relayed by Dex from an unnamed attendee (Chatham House); he does not say he does this himself.
cards.landing: Recurring defect shapes become CI lint rules / import-linter contracts rather than new CLAUDE.md lines
cards.inventory_ref: (B) August 2026 - AI That Works #69 Unconference Recap

cards.author: other
cards.quote: if you can just write a list of a hundred rules of like this should never happen
cards.claim: A small cheap fast model given a list of about 100 'should never happen' rules is nearly as good as a deterministic linter, easier to maintain, at higher cost and latency.
cards.evidence_detail: Someone cited DeepSeek V4 Flash; Dex relays it; Vaibhav adds a $5 review against $1000 per feature argument.
cards.landing: Cheap-model rule-list reviewer as a middle tier between lint and Opus reviewer
cards.inventory_ref: (B) August 2026 - AI That Works #69 Unconference Recap

cards.author: Dex
cards.quote: you should not like stop reading the code until you're very confident
cards.claim: Aim for lights-off but keep reading all code until you have merged on the order of a thousand PRs over a month or two with no feedback needed.
cards.evidence_detail: Dex goes from 50% to 90% unreviewed merges as an example; ambitious goals are fine but confidence must be earned.
cards.landing: Owner-review gate and criteria for loosening it
cards.inventory_ref: (B) August 2026 - AI That Works #69 Unconference Recap

cards.author: Kyle
cards.quote: Read the least amount of code you need to ship reliable software.
cards.claim: If you do not read the code you cannot claim it is good; best engineers in a large code base still read only the minimum needed.
cards.evidence_detail: Dex reads aloud a tweet by Kyle Mistele.
cards.landing: Owner view: what to read vs what verifiers cover
cards.inventory_ref: (B) August 2026 - AI That Works #69 Unconference Recap

cards.author: Dex
cards.quote: adversarial review does not solve your problem.
cards.claim: Saying 'adversarial' is not magic: adversarial review catches the dumb stuff and slightly improves code but does not fix slop, even though nearly everyone runs some such loop before a human sees the diff.
cards.evidence_detail: Dex pushes back on Vaibhav's observation that almost everyone shipping with AI had an adversarial loop to delay human review.
cards.landing: Refuter and Opus-reviewer design: what it can and cannot be relied on to catch
cards.inventory_ref: (B) August 2026 - AI That Works #69 Unconference Recap

cards.author: Dex
cards.quote: take a plan that you already know was implemented well, change the skill, and then just see if it still implements well.
cards.claim: Evaluate skills by replaying a known-good plan through the implement loop with one skill changed, because plan, skills and environment are the only variables.
cards.evidence_detail: Dex restates an unconference talk (Vaibhav's takeaway) and ties it to AITW #1 on breaking big problems into probe-able parts.
cards.landing: Regression-test harness for new skills and saved workflows using a frozen past phase
cards.inventory_ref: (B) August 2026 - AI That Works #69 Unconference Recap

cards.author: other
cards.quote: review what rent what went wrong, pull in PR comments, pull in agent traces, pull in user messages
cards.claim: A three-skill loop (discuss/decide, implement, compound) where the compound step weekly collects PR comments, traces and user messages into a report of what humans had to fix, and a couple items per week are built into the plan or implement skills.
cards.evidence_detail: Unnamed attendee's talk; Dex says it was 'very good'.
cards.landing: Weekly retrospective that turns the decisions journal and review findings into harness changes
cards.inventory_ref: (B) August 2026 - AI That Works #69 Unconference Recap

cards.author: other
cards.quote: You change the reasoning, you change one of the earliest tokens in your whole prompt. Everything is invalidated.
cards.claim: Switching reasoning effort mid-conversation changes an early token in the prompt and invalidates the whole prompt cache.
cards.evidence_detail: Shown from a GPT-OSS-style prompt template; Dex initially doubted it, then accepted it. Not verified for every provider.
cards.landing: Set effort at session start per role; do not toggle mid-session
cards.inventory_ref: (B) August 2026 - AI That Works #69 Unconference Recap

cards.author: Dex
cards.quote: changes the chance that the next token will be more reasoning
cards.claim: A reasoning-level setting works like any other instruction, shifting the probability of more reasoning tokens, and low/medium/high are semantic hints rather than hard limits.
cards.evidence_detail: Dex's explanation after Vaibhav notes models trained on medium/high still respond to 'low'.
cards.landing: Effort routing expectations
cards.inventory_ref: (B) August 2026 - AI That Works #69 Unconference Recap

cards.author: Dex
cards.quote: don't store your artifacts in Git.
cards.claim: Plans, research and specs should be git-ignored and synced to an external store, because in-repo plan files go stale, are lost across branches and worktrees, and GitHub can only comment on diffs.
cards.evidence_detail: The progression Dex says many customers and his own team went through: plan.md, plans folder, per-feature folders, then 'what branch was that plan on?'.
cards.landing: Where the ship plan, decisions journal and knowledge store live (docs/program in Git today)
cards.inventory_ref: (B) August 2026 - AI That Works #69 Unconference Recap

cards.author: Dex
cards.quote: the model finds them but they're out of date. and so like it actually like slows you down
cards.claim: Accumulated plan documents that agents discover become stale context that makes work slower rather than faster.
cards.evidence_detail: Part of the artifacts-in-Git progression; fix attempts were per-feature scoping and cleanup after shipping.
cards.landing: Expiry or archival rule for plan docs; knowledge-store design for verified diagnoses
cards.inventory_ref: (B) August 2026 - AI That Works #69 Unconference Recap

cards.author: Dex
cards.quote: you don't need any extra MCP tools.
cards.claim: Sync artifacts to the local file system through a harness hook so the agent reads and writes ordinary files, with no extra MCP tools; CRDTs are probably unnecessary because scrappy file sync suffices.
cards.evidence_detail: How HumanLayer works (hook pushes to an API, a daemon watcher syncs down); admits one unhandled race; a second-generation approach was a hard-linked context repo with a commit-time push/pull and no branching.
cards.landing: Hook-based artifact sync (re-opens the skipped hooks decision) vs plain files
cards.inventory_ref: (B) August 2026 - AI That Works #69 Unconference Recap

cards.author: Dex
cards.quote: reverse engineered it into seven small PRs. Seven small PRs of like three to five K each.
cards.claim: Prototype a feature as one large unattended PR, then use that code as the spec to write a PR-splitting plan and rebuild it as small reviewable PRs, each in a fresh worktree with the prototype as reference.
cards.evidence_detail: A 20,000-line overnight Fable run split into seven PRs of 1.5-5k lines; planning took 1-2 hours; Kyle reviews the small PRs.
cards.landing: Phase PR sizing and a PR-splitting step; saved workflow for splitting
cards.inventory_ref: (B) August 2026 - AI That Works #69 Unconference Recap

cards.author: Dex
cards.quote: I don't even use Ralph loops anymore. I just use in human layer you can queue up a bunch of messages
cards.claim: Overnight runs can be driven by queuing messages (a progress prompt file, /compact, 'keep going', a Codex review-and-fix skill) instead of a Ralph loop.
cards.evidence_detail: One feature built overnight from a PRD and an HTML mock-up covering every dropdown, loading and error state; then an hour or two of hand polishing.
cards.landing: Phase-routine scripting: queued prompts with compaction between steps
cards.inventory_ref: (B) August 2026 - AI That Works #69 Unconference Recap

cards.author: Dex
cards.quote: we kind of force it to like repeat code if we don't know what the abstractions are.
cards.claim: When riffing a new feature, keep it in its own tree, forbid changing shared code (no extra props or parameters), copy functions into the new tree, and discard the old tree later.
cards.evidence_detail: Used for the 20k-line prototype; also 'copy the file and delete from it rather than reading the file and writing the new code'.
cards.landing: Slice-boundary rules for agent work on new vertical slices
cards.inventory_ref: (B) August 2026 - AI That Works #69 Unconference Recap

cards.author: Dex
cards.quote: AI knows it too well
cards.claim: Models over-apply design patterns (factory everywhere) or over-complicate algorithms, so teaching patterns is not the gap.
cards.evidence_detail: Answer to 'do we need design patterns if the AI knows them'.
cards.landing: Do not add pattern primers to CLAUDE.md
cards.inventory_ref: (B) August 2026 - AI That Works #69 Unconference Recap

cards.author: Dex
cards.quote: the model tools are not good.
cards.claim: For editing rich documents the model's tools are poor; his team had the model write a markdown edit and a small model convert it into a QuickJS snippet (code-mode style).
cards.evidence_detail: Answer to a Google Docs question; marked as needing Kyle for details.
cards.landing: Small-model helper for mechanical edits
cards.inventory_ref: (B) August 2026 - AI That Works #69 Unconference Recap

cards.source_title: AI That Works #70 syncs and A/B testing 200 agents
cards.author: Dex
cards.quote: after a hundred features, my code base will be like 40% slop.
cards.claim: A roughly 10-12% bad-decision rate per feature compounds on the code base itself, so unattended factories degrade toward unrecoverable at a few dozen features.
cards.evidence_detail: Dex's arithmetic on Avery's 12.5% figure (the chance of a mistake also depends on how clean the code base already is); not a measurement of his own.
cards.landing: Why per-phase verification and a refuter run before merge; budget for debt repayment phases
cards.inventory_ref: (B) August 2026 - AI That Works #70 (listed as 'Syncs and A/B Testing 200 Agents')

cards.source_title: AI That Works #70 syncs and A/B testing 200 agents
cards.author: other
cards.quote: 12.5% of runs introduced a second source of truth for time tracking
cards.claim: In 200 runs per feature, 12.5% added a second source of truth (e.g. system vs wall time) on the holds feature, and every test stayed green so CI could not catch it.
cards.evidence_detail: Avery (Boundary): Codex GPT-5.6 Sol high, Ticketmaster in Rust built one feature at a time; Dex repeats the figure and draws the compounding conclusion.
cards.landing: Green tests are not evidence of design quality; reviewer must inspect data structures
cards.inventory_ref: (B) August 2026 - AI That Works #70 (listed as 'Syncs and A/B Testing 200 Agents')

cards.source_title: AI That Works #70 syncs and A/B testing 200 agents
cards.author: other
cards.quote: Roughly forty percent of agents made a manual index map
cards.claim: For 'stable seat order', about 40% of runs kept a separate ordering vector (a second source of truth) while 35% used a self-ordering map; some used two boolean flags permitting impossible states.
cards.evidence_detail: Same 200-run experiment; Avery argues all slop starts as bad data structures and that giving all features up front or reviewing data structures are the fixes.
cards.landing: Reviewer prompt item: check for duplicated state and representable-illegal-state
cards.inventory_ref: (B) August 2026 - AI That Works #70 (listed as 'Syncs and A/B Testing 200 Agents')

cards.source_title: AI That Works #70 syncs and A/B testing 200 agents
cards.author: Dex
cards.quote: You just land in a raw code base.
cards.claim: SlopCodeBench gives each checkpoint a raw checkout with no commit history or prior context, deliberately, so the agent must investigate what it inherited.
cards.evidence_detail: Dex corrects Avery on benchmark setup; 'it's intentional'.
cards.landing: Cold-resume trial design: repo state only, no history
cards.inventory_ref: (B) August 2026 - AI That Works #70 (listed as 'Syncs and A/B Testing 200 Agents')

cards.source_title: AI That Works #70 syncs and A/B testing 200 agents
cards.author: Kyle
cards.quote: you don't want to write to the API, write that to Postgres, wait for it to go out on the replication log
cards.claim: HumanLayer keeps two sync paths: structured rows through Postgres's write-ahead log, and token streaming through a separate durable stream server so high-frequency updates do not load the database.
cards.evidence_detail: Kyle Mistele's architecture walk-through (Electric SQL, Caddy durable-streams plugin, SSE); product internals, little bearing on the harness.
cards.landing: nowhere obvious
cards.inventory_ref: (B) August 2026 - AI That Works #70 (listed as 'Syncs and A/B Testing 200 Agents')

gaps: meta.md files contain only episode descriptions; no extra ideas.
Transcripts are auto-captions with unlabeled speakers; in episode 70 Avery speaks through Vaibhav's mic, so attribution of the 200-run experiment relies on README and context.
Dex's referenced charts, the SlopCodeBench report files and Kyle's tweet were not opened; numbers are as spoken.
Episode 70's sync-engine half (Kyle) was only lightly carded because it has little bearing on the harness.
Cards 25, 26, 31 and 32 carry other people's ideas that Dex relays or accepts rather than argues.

new_sources.title: humanlayer/skills repository (referred to in AITW #68 as the team's skills)
new_sources.why: Already in inventory; mentioned only as context, nothing new.
